questions.question: Why do activations often become the real memory bottleneck during transformer training?
options: Because backward needs many intermediate tensors from every layer, and their volume grows with batch, sequence length, and hidden size
Because activations are always stored in FP64
Because optimizers do not require any extra memory
Because only embeddings are differentiable
questions.explanation: The lesson emphasizes that backprop must retain inputs and derivative-relevant intermediates, not just model weights. On long contexts, those saved tensors can outweigh the weight and optimizer memory by a large margin.

questions.question: What tradeoff does gradient checkpointing make?
options: More memory for less compute
Less memory in exchange for extra recomputation FLOPs during backward
Less memory by shrinking the model's vocabulary
More throughput by skipping gradient computation
questions.explanation: Checkpointing stores only selected boundary activations during forward. When backward needs missing intermediates, it reruns parts of the forward pass, saving memory while paying extra compute.

questions.question: According to the lesson's cost model, what is the approximate FLOP overhead of naive full checkpointing?
options: About 5%
About 15%
About 33%
About 100%
questions.explanation: The lesson models a normal step as forward plus backward, roughly 3 units of layer FLOPs. Full checkpointing adds about one extra forward worth of recompute, raising that to 4 units, which is about a one-third overhead.

questions.question: Why can selective checkpointing be much cheaper than checkpointing whole layers?
options: It recomputes only the most memory-expensive parts such as attention instead of the whole layer
It avoids the backward pass on feed-forward networks
It works only when activations are offloaded to CPU
It reduces parameter count so less recomputation is needed
questions.explanation: Not all saved tensors cost the same amount of memory. The lesson highlights that quadratic attention intermediates dominate long-context memory, so recomputing just those pieces can save most of the memory for only a small extra compute cost.

questions.question: For uniform-cost layers, what segment-size heuristic does the lesson cite as the classic memory/compute balance?
options: Checkpoint every layer twice
Use about sqrt(L) checkpoint segments for L layers
Never checkpoint the middle layers
Set the segment size equal to the vocabulary size
questions.explanation: The Chen et al. style rule of thumb is to break an L-layer stack into about sqrt(L) segments. The lesson presents that as the classic compromise where memory and recompute both scale like the square root rather than linearly.
